# rMQR Decoder

Design record for the rMQR Code (ISO/IEC 23941) decode feature (`RmQRCodeDecoder`): what it does, why it is scoped the way it is, and what was learned while building it. The [spec-to-code map](rmqr-spec-map.md) indexes where each part is implemented. The encoder side is in [rMQR Encoder](rmqr-encoder.md). The work followed the rMQR implementation plan, which has since been folded into this record and the [spec-to-code map](rmqr-spec-map.md).

Status: **matrix level shipped (Phase 6, 2026-08-15). Image level shipped (Phase 7, 2026-08-16). Adversarial review on 2026-08-16: format arbitration now takes the dimensions into account, a destination too small for the result is terminal for that finder, and the perspective quadratic was fixed (see Decisions and Lessons learned below).**

---

## What

`RmQRCodeDecoder` decodes rMQR symbols back into text.

### Matrix level

Input: `RmQRCodeData`, or a span with one byte per module plus its `width` and `height` (the format `RmQRCodeGenerator.Create(Span<byte>)` produces). The matrix may have a light quiet zone or none. Borders are stripped automatically, whether uniform or asymmetric.

Behavior: the decoder takes the version from the physical dimensions, then reads both format-information copies. It removes the fixed mask and walks the inverse zigzag, deinterleaves the blocks, and corrects each block with Reed-Solomon. Finally it parses the bit stream into text (Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte, with ECI segments parsed). Diagnostics are reported in `RmQRCodeDecodeInfo`: status, version, ECC level and corrected codewords. The overloads mirror `MicroQRCodeDecoder`: one returns a string, and an allocation-free variant writes to a span destination sized by `GetMaxDecodedLength(version)`.

### Image level

Input: an `SKBitmap`, or a grayscale luminance span with its width and height (`TryDecodeImage`). An allocation-free variant writes to a span destination. When the version is unknown, size it with `GetMaxDecodedLength(RmQRVersion.R17x139)`.

Behavior: the same path runs in each of the [shared image decode passes](qrcode-symbologies.md#image-decode-passes). The passes are the global threshold, the inverted image, the regional binarization of each polarity, and a sweep at the midpoint of the grey levels for a polarity whose global pass found no finder. In each pass, the steps are:

- The [shared candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan) ranks the finder candidates.
- Local grid frames are built around the finder. The four right angles come first, each also transposed for mirroring. Then come the frames of the finder's own outline, measured off the inner edges of its light ring, including any shear that perspective gives it. Last comes the angular sweep of the finder axis, for arbitrary rotation.
- At low density, each frame first reads a table of module boundaries off the timing lines, and that table is decoded on its own.
- The finder-side format copy is sampled in the frame. It gives the version, and therefore the symbol's width and height, before any grid is fitted.
- The sub-finder is located near the corner the version predicts. It anchors the far end of the symbol, which gives the global scale and rotation in closed form.
- Affine grids are tried.
- When the frame's copy read an exact codeword, the perimeter is traced from the frame. The timing patterns of the top row, the left column and the bottom row are followed run by run from the finder, and one homography is fitted to their edges.
- Once an anchored grid gets past its format information, a bounded projective search runs over two projective coefficients and the row-axis shear. Each time, the column scale and rotation are solved again from the sub-finder. The row pitch is not solved: it is taken from the frame's own scale. The sub-finder-side format copy and the edge timing patterns gate the search.
- Each sampled grid goes to the matrix decoder above. On grey edges, a re-read by coverage follows.

When no anchored grid gets past its format information, as when the sub-finder is not found, the unrefined frame is decoded. The [spec-to-code map](rmqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling) draws the stages and their order.

On success, the result carries the symbol's four corners in image coordinates (`RmQRCodeDecodeInfo.Corners`; the contract is in [qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md#public-api-direction)). They come from the transform of the frame that read. The frames handle a mirrored capture by swapping their axes, not by transposing the sampled grid. So that transform is always in symbol order, and the corners never need swapping.

How close the corners lie depends on the grid that read. A grid anchored on the sub-finder reads a keystone through error correction without following it, so its far corners carry the remaining error. A traced grid is fitted to the symbol's own edges, its outer edge included. The worst corner error, measured at 8 px per module against the rendered scene (every version, an edge shortened at both ends, 2026-09-28):

- Top edge shortened 1 % a side: 0.97 module. At 2 %: 1.27 (R7x99; 7 of 32 versions past a module). At 3 %: 1.55. At 4 %: 1.67. At 6 %: 1.81. At 8 %: 1.86 (R17x43). At 10 %: 2.10 (R11x27). Each of these worst cases is a read the decoder made the same way before the trace was added.
- Top edge shortened 12 and 15 %, read only since the trace was added: 0.59 and 0.47.
- Left edge shortened: 0.67 or less up to 4 %, and 0.16 or less from 6 to 15 %.

The contract therefore states about a module under perspective, and about two from 2 % up. Tracing the perimeter from the winning grid after a read would bring those reads down to the traced figures. A trace costs about as much as a clean decode (20 µs at R17x139), so that is left as a follow-up.

### Image decode figures

These figures show how the decoder reads each kind of input. [decode_figures.cs](../../../tools/decode_figures.cs) draws them from the library's own symbols and decodes each input through the public API, so no figure can show a read that does not happen. Rerun it when the pipeline changes.

#### Stage by stage

A clean R11x43 on the main path.

![Stage by stage: luminance, global threshold, finder candidates, finder-side format copy, sub-finder, isotropic grid](../images/rmqr/decode-overview.svg)

- **Luminance:** the grey input.
- **Global threshold:** one Otsu split of the histogram into ink and paper.
- **Finder candidates:** patterns that read 1:1:3:1:1 along a line through their centre and pass the cross-checks, most confirmed first.
- **Finder-side format copy:** read beside the finder before any grid is fitted. It gives the version, and so the width and height.
- **Sub-finder:** searched for near the corner the version predicts.
- **Isotropic grid:** a single rotation and a single scale map the finder centre onto the sub-finder centre, and the grid is sampled at every module.

#### Reading the input figures

Each figure shows the input, with what the decoder finds drawn over it, above the path through the [image-level stages](rmqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling). Every pass runs this path: the global threshold, the inverted image, the regional pass, then the midpoint sweep (see [image decode passes](qrcode-symbologies.md#image-decode-passes)). A mirrored capture is read by a frame with its axes swapped. No grid is read transposed.

Green and grey boxes run for this input. Green marks the stages it depends on.

- **Key** (green): without this stage, the input would not read, or would read only after more grids fail than with it. A grid is one sampling, and its coverage read counts as the same grid.
- **Runs** (grey): runs as for any input.
- **Only if needed** (dashed): runs only when the grids before it fail.
- **Skipped** (faded): does not run for this input.

The numbers on the boxes match the numbered notes.

#### Clean

An upright, crisp R11x77.

![Clean R11x77 and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-clean.svg)

The format copy reads at the measured scale and gives R11x77. The sub-finder is where that version puts it, and the isotropic grid anchored on it reads first. The image has only two grey levels, so the grey-level stages stay off. At this density the boundary table is not used.

#### Rotated or mirrored

An R11x77, turned and seen in a mirror.

![Rotated and mirrored R11x77 and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-rotated.svg)

1. **Finder outline:** the axis-aligned frames sample no grid. Starting from the angular sweep, the inner edges of the finder's light ring give the finder's own axes. One of the outline's frames, with its axes swapped, reads the format copy. That is how the mirror is read.
2. **Perimeter trace:** from that frame, the top row, the left column and the bottom row are followed run by run, and the grid fitted to their edges reads. Without the outline, a sweep frame and its isotropic grid read the symbol, after the same number of grids.

#### Keystone distortion

An R11x77 in perspective, its top edge shortened by 16 %, 8 % at each end.

![Keystoned R11x77 and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-keystone.svg)

1. **Finder outline:** the columns lean 30° at the finder. The square frame built from the finder's runs (dashed) misplaces the format copy, so no axis-aligned frame reads it. The outline of the light ring includes the lean, and one of its frames reads the copy.
2. **Perimeter trace:** each dark run of the top row, the left column and the bottom row is found where the step of the runs before it predicts. One homography fitted to their edges reads with no correction. Without the trace, nothing reads.

With the top edge shortened 4 % at each end, the perspective search anchored on the sub-finder reads this symbol through error correction, before the outline is measured. At 8 %, only the trace reads it.

#### Non-square modules

An upright R11x77 whose modules are wider than tall.

![R11x77 with non-square modules and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-non-square.svg)

1. **Axis-aligned frames:** the module size is measured separately along each axis, from a dark-light-dark run through the finder centre that spans six modules. Without the two separate sizes, the outline's frame reads, after one more failed grid.

The isotropic grid scales the frame uniformly, so it keeps both sizes and reads first. The anisotropic grid is not needed.

#### Grey edges

An anti-aliased R11x77 at about one and a half pixels per module, slightly turned.

![Anti-aliased R11x77 and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-grey-edges.svg)

1. **Sub-finder:** found several modules from where the version predicts it, and refined to its centre.
2. **Isotropic grid:** its rotation, set by the line from the finder to the sub-finder, follows the symbol's turn. The axis-aligned frame does not.
3. **Coverage re-read:** the grid fails but gets past its format information, so it is read again. This time each module's luminance is interpolated at its centre and split halfway between the two levels. That read succeeds.

#### Hidden sub-finder

An upright R11x77 whose sub-finder is painted out, as damage or a label would.

![R11x77 with its sub-finder painted out, and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-hidden-sub-finder.svg)

1. **Perimeter trace:** no sub-finder is found, so no grid can be anchored on one. The trace needs no sub-finder. It finds the runs of the three edges it follows all the way to the painted-out corner, and the grid fitted to them reads.
2. **Unrefined frame:** without the trace, the frame at the scale that read the format copy is sampled on its own, and it reads the symbol after the same number of grids.

#### Snapped scale

A crisp R11x77 at a non-integer scale, with modules snapped to whole pixels.

![R11x77 at a snapped scale and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-snapped.svg)

1. **Finder-side format copy:** the scale measured at the finder is a few percent over the symbol's pitch, and at that scale the copy does not decode. At a scale a few percent smaller, it reads and gives the version.
2. **Sub-finder:** found about a module from where the version predicts it. The isotropic grid anchored on it corrects the scale and reads. Without the sub-finder, the perimeter traced from the same frame reads, after the same number of grids.

#### Low density

A crisp R11x77 at a little over one pixel per module.

![R11x77 at low density and its path through the pipeline](../images/rmqr/decode-input-low-density.svg)

1. **Finder candidates:** the row-strided scan misses the finder, and the sweep of every row finds it.
2. **Low density:** each module is one or two whole pixels, a pattern a fitted grid rarely follows. So the module boundaries are read along the top row and the left column, and each module is sampled between its own boundaries. The width and height counted from the boundaries give the version, and this grid reads before the format copy is tried. Two-pixel modules are marked.

### Supported

| Area | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Versions | All 32 (R7x43 … R17x139), identified by width × height and cross-checked against the format information |
| ECC levels | M, H |
| Data modes | Numeric, Alphanumeric, Byte (the same UTF-8 / ISO-8859-1 heuristics as the other symbologies), Kanji (JIS X 0208; the generator writes it for text that JIS X 0208 covers), ECI headers 1 / 3 / 26 / 27 |
| Quiet zone | Matrix: any light border, uniform or not (the bounding box of the dark modules is the core). Image: 1, 2 and 4 modules verified. The finder scan needs some light margin around the finder |
| Error correction | Reed-Solomon per block, at full strength (⌊ecc/2⌋ codewords per block). Corrections are reported |
| Format information | Matrix: either copy alone is enough, with ≤ 3 bit errors per copy corrected. Only copies that give the same version as the dimensions count, and the closer of those wins, so a copy miscorrected toward another version's word cannot veto the valid one. Image: the finder-side copy must be readable (≤ 3 bit errors), because it gives the version before any grid is fitted (at low density, the counted width × height gives it instead). The sub-finder-side copy is a consistency gate on the perspective path. Each sampled grid then goes through the matrix decoder, which arbitrates between both copies as on the matrix path |
| Output | `string` (allocates only the result) or `Span<char>` (no allocation in steady state, image path included) |
| Image envelope | Clean renders of every version × ECC at 3-13 px/module and at non-integer scales. A shading gradient or a soft-edged shadow over part of the symbol (images at least 33 px a side; measured in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md)). Every version at 1.5-6 px/module in four rotations. Pixel-aligned renders from 1 px/module. Non-square modules within the envelope shared with the other symbologies ([qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md)). Translation. Right-angle and arbitrary rotation (every integer degree verified for R7x43 / R13x77). Mirroring. Reflectance reversal. JPEG q60, low contrast, additive noise. Rings printed or read thicker or thinner than their modules (ink spread, a thin print, blur), which the shared finder check finds through the distances between edges of the same polarity ([qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md), drawn in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#thin-or-thick-rings)). Symbols whose dark edges all moved by 0.1, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.24 of a module (every version, 3-6 px/module, turned 0-60°, grey or binarized) read 597, 588, 454 and 193 of 600. Extreme aspect ratios. Keystone to 20 % at 2-6 px/module in any turn, mirrored too, narrowed along either axis or toward a corner. Of those narrowed along the short axis at 3-6 px/module, 1,278 of 1,280 renders read: widths 99 and 139 read 240 and 238 of 240, and the two that fail are R7x139 sheared 41° at the finder, which the scan does not find. Stronger keystone at 3-6 px/module: 377 of 384 read at 20-40 %, and 159 of 192 at 40-50 %. Crisp renders at 8 px/module with an edge shortened up to 8 % a side, every version except R7x139 and R9x139 at 8 %, whose columns lean 58° and 51° at the finder. The 148-symbol external PNG corpus |

The [image decode sweep](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#image-decode-sweep) compares this library with zxing-cpp 0.5.2 on the same images (2026-09-28; 640 cases, twenty a version, each encoded by this library and by libzint, 1,280 renders of each kind). This library reads 28,656 of 29,440 and zxing-cpp reads 7,771. zxing-cpp reads no render that this library does not. This library reads 1,272 to 1,280 of 1,280 in every kind except anti-aliased edges at 1.0-1.25 px/module, where it reads 510. zxing-cpp reads at most 1,130 of any kind, and none of the mirrored renders. On the real images, both read 12 of 12.

### Not supported

- ECI assignments other than the four above (`UnsupportedContent`).
- FNC1 and Structured Append. They are not defined for rMQR and have no mode indicators, so no rMQR stream can carry them (the reserved indicators are `InvalidBitstream`).
- Kanji cells outside the JIS X 0208 repertoire, which are reported separately as `UnmappedCharacter`.
- Keystone past 40 %, and past 20 % below 3 px/module. Measured: 170 of 192 read at 20-40 %, and 159 of 192 at 40-50 % from 3 px/module. Of the renders left, 22 find no finder and 33 fail in the data.
- Hard-edged shadows, blur, and heavily styled symbols below about 5 px/module. Gradients make the finder runs too fuzzy. The same styling decodes at 8+ px/module.

## Why

- Explicitly typed decoder (no auto-detection inside `QRCodeDecoder`): the reasoning is the same as for Micro QR. Standard QR scanning performance and behavior stay unchanged, and a caller who has an rMQR matrix knows it.
- Version from the dimensions, not from the format information alone: a matrix whose format copies decode to another version is corrupt (or wrongly cropped), not a smaller symbol. Rejecting the contradiction (`FormatInformationInvalid`) is the safer default.
- Dark-bounding-box quiet-zone stripping: the bounding box of the dark modules is exactly the core, so no uniform border has to be assumed. That holds because rMQR has dark modules at all four core corners (the finder, two corner patterns and the sub-finder) and timing patterns on every edge. Micro QR needed the finder-corner trick because its right and bottom edges are data.
- Format first, then geometry: every full grid sample is made with the dimensions already known. An rMQR symbol has 32 possible sizes, so trying every size in each frame (the Micro QR approach, over 4 sizes) would mean 8× more sampling. The finder-side format copy carries the version, and it sits within 12 modules of the finder, where even a coarse local frame reads it reliably.
- Sub-finder as the far anchor: the scale estimate at the finder is accurate to a pixel over a 12-module span (±2 % measured when it was a 7-module span, before its edges were paired by polarity). That is 2-3 modules of error at the far end of a 139-module symbol. The fitted axis is good to about half a degree. Neither is usable over that baseline. The sub-finder is a precise far point (a 5×5 template on a half-module lattice, then the midpoint of the center dark module). So the scale along the finder→sub-finder line and the frame rotation come out exactly, in closed form, for any candidate projective coefficients.
- Row-axis shear as a searched parameter: a keystone leans the finder's column axis by atan(shrink / height): 9° at 2 % on 17 rows, 14° at 4 %. The sub-finder fixes the column direction, since the finder→sub-finder line is almost a symbol row, but it leaves the row axis free. So the row axis is searched (±20° in 1° steps) alongside the two projective coefficients. It is not measured, because a 1-module feature at 8 px cannot be measured to the precision needed.
- The perimeter as the measure of strong perspective: every edge of an rMQR symbol is a timing pattern, so the symbol shows its own perspective all round its perimeter. Following the perimeter run by run, with each run looked for where the step of the runs before it predicts, measures what a frame at the finder can only extrapolate. Across 139 modules, a keystone changes the module pitch by a quarter and leans the columns up to 40° at the finder, beyond the search's ±12 % and ±20°. One least-squares homography over a few hundred edges averages out each edge's pixel rounding, and no sub-finder is needed.
- The finder's own outline before the sweep's frames: the sweep's frames are square, but a finder in strong perspective is a parallelogram, and a square frame on it puts the format copy a module or two off. The inner edges of the finder's light ring bound the ring whatever surrounds the pattern, so neither a quiet zone nor a separator is assumed. Where the centre chord meets those edges tells a finder from a 5 × 5 pattern of rings (a sub-finder or an alignment pattern). Every finder that the axis-aligned frames do not read gets its outline's frames first, whether it is square or not. A rotated symbol reads through them as soon as through a sweep frame. A symbol narrowed along its width, whose finder stays square, reads in about half the time.
- Cheap gates before every full sample on the perspective path: the first gate is the sub-finder-side format copy (18 samples), which must decode to the same version within distance 1. The second is the edge timing patterns between the anchors (rows 0 and h−1), which must alternate. Wrong coefficients bend the middle of the symbol even when both anchors are right. Without the timing gate, the search used up its full-decode budget on grids that were right at both anchors and wrong in between.
- Correction capacity as a table, not an expression: `RmQRConstants.GetErrorCorrectionCapacity` holds all 64 version × ECC values, and the matrix decoder applies them per block, in the same shape as `MicroQRMatrixDecoder`. Every entry is the full RS strength `t = ⌊ecc/2⌋`, because rMQR appears to reserve no misdecode-protection codewords `p` of the kind Micro QR has. So the cap can never take effect today. It exists so that both symbologies read the rule from the same place, and so that a reserved `p` would only be a data edit. The evidence for `p = 0` is indirect (the block structure and zxing-cpp's behaviour), not a reading of Table 8. See Decisions.

## Decisions

| Decision | Choice | Revisit when |
|---|---|---|
| Correction cap | A per-block cap, read from a 64-row capacity table and applied after correction (as `MicroQRMatrixDecoder` does). Every entry is `t = ⌊ecc/2⌋`, because no misdecode-protection codewords `p` appear to be reserved. So the cap has no effect today, and the table is where a future `p` would go. **The ISO/IEC 23941 Table 8 capacity column has not been read**: the standard is paywalled, and the public preview stops short of it. Supporting evidence: the oracle-verified block structure leaves ≤ 1 unused ECC codeword per block on all 64 rows (60 of them have an even ECC count, where any `p ≥ 1` would lower `t`). And `tools/QRInteropFixtures -- probe-rmqr-capacity` measured zxing-cpp agreeing with our capacity in both directions on all 64 rows (2026-08-21, see [QR Test Fixtures](qrcode-test-fixtures.md)). Checked and rejected as a source (2026-08-21): the [Wikipedia rMQR article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangular_Micro_QR_Code) has no capacity, block-count or `p` column at all. Its version table agrees with ours 64/64 on data and ECC codewords, which only confirms the input to the derivation. Its prose claim that rMQR uses "1 to 4 blocks" is wrong: R15x139-H has 5, R17x139-H has 6, and 4 blocks there would need 39 ECC codewords per block, above the 30 the RS generators go up to. So it is not a reliable transcription of Table 8 | Someone reads Table 8 in the published standard (**still open**: do this before a release that advertises rMQR conformance), or `probe-rmqr-capacity` starts failing against a newer zxing-cpp |
| Format copy arbitration | Matrix: only copies whose version matches the dimensions are candidates. The closer one wins, and a tie goes to the finder side. (Review 2026-08-16: arbitrating before the dimension check let a copy miscorrected toward another version's word veto the valid copy.) Image: the finder-side copy gives the version, and the sub-finder-side copy only gates the perspective path | Image-level recovery from a damaged finder-side copy. It would need a sub-finder-side read for each candidate version, through a frame that is only accurate near the finder, and only narrow symbols would benefit |
| ECI on decode | Parsed (by the shared reader, moved into `SegmentDecoders`) and mapped to ISO-8859-1 / UTF-8. Other assignments report `UnsupportedContent` | Demand for other charsets (cross-symbology decision) |
| Corpus expectations | libzint symbols decode with 0 corrections, and qrtool symbols with ≤ 1 (a documented tail defect). The same holds through the image path | qrtool fixes the defect (then regenerate, and tighten to 0) |
| Image search budgets | The shared scan's 8 finder candidates ([single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan)). ≤ 256 full-grid decodes per candidate. A sub-finder search radius of 6 + width/20 modules (half-module lattice, three column-axis leans). A perspective grid of ±12 % (1 % steps along the width, 2 % along the height) × ±20° shear | A measured input class needs more (then raise the constant and add its test), or profiling shows the budget dominates a common failure |
| Sub-finder search order | Outward ring by ring, stopping at the first perfect 25/25 match | Noisy inputs where the true position scores < 25 while a nearer position scores 25 (none observed) |
| Perspective search gate | The search opens once the isotropic or the anisotropic grid gets past its format information. The unrefined frame runs after both and cannot open it. Letting the unrefined frame open the search when neither grid got that far was measured (2026-09-27). It reads 7 of the 14 failing 4 % keystones, one of them in the tests' renderer, and loses no read in the envelope or the test suite. But it makes failing decodes far slower: 2.1 to 6.2 times on Standard QR images of versions 7 to 14, whose alignment patterns are found as sub-finders; 1.5 times on 640 × 480 noise; and up to 12 times on rMQR past 8 % keystone. The frame reads the finder-side format copy through the same samples that gave the version, so it gets past the format information even on a Standard QR image. Also requiring the sub-finder-side copy, read through that frame, to give the version removes the cost, since the gate then opened on no failing input. But it keeps only 1 of the 7 reads, because under a keystone that frame is off at the far end | A condition that tells a keystoned rMQR from a Standard QR image or noise, measured against a tolerance of +3 % on common failures (no symbol, another symbology, an rMQR past correction) and at most twice the time on any unreadable distorted rMQR |
| Strong perspective | The perimeter trace (see Why) runs in two places. It runs from each frame of the finder's outline, after the axis-aligned frames and before the sweep's. It also runs in each axis-aligned or sweep frame whose copy read an exact codeword, after the isotropic and anisotropic grids and before the perspective search. Each part was changed on the final code and measured (2026-09-28, about 3,700 renders: strong keystones at 2-6 px/module, plain, blurred, and at low contrast with noise; the crisp scenes; rotations; and keystones to 6 %). The net reads lost for each part: the walk put back across the line after each run, 560; the outline, 179; edges at the threshold instead of the midpoint of the levels, 146; the perspective search, 115 (it is kept, behind the trace); the step set to each run's own instead of moved halfway to it, 49; the trace in the axis-aligned and sweep frames, 37; the outer edge looked for within 0.35 or 0.6 of a module instead of 0.45, 13 and 4; run ends within 0.8 of a module instead of one, 12 at the near end and 4 at the far end; an outline frame's copy held to an exact codeword, 10; the outline not measured again along its own axes, 6. Starting the trace in the axis-aligned and sweep frames only from an exact copy reads 1 render fewer than starting it from any copy that decodes. It also takes 4 % less time on other symbologies' images, and 1 % less on the failure set. Counting a failed traced grid as the frame's result read the same, except for one anti-aliased render at 1.31 px/module, which it lost by ending the search over scales. Skipping a trace where another frame of the finder had already traced the same side read 35 fewer of 800 noisy keystones. Running the outline first for every finder, not only for one sheared 3° or more, read the same, and read long-axis keystones in about half the time. Measured and removed: the outline's seed axes swapped (−2 +2); the finder centre as a point of the fit (no difference measured); the left column's outer edge as points of the fit (no difference measured, corners no better); four chords a side instead of two (no difference). As before, there is no false read on 200,000 images of noise and other symbologies | A distortion the trace cannot follow: an edge's timing pattern lost over three runs in a row, a symbol bent off the plane, or a finder sheared past about 45° (where R7x139 and R9x139 read their version and every grid fails). Or the outline's measurement becoming the cost of rotated reads (2.5 % now) |
| Failed-decode cost | Two guards on `TryLocateSubFinder` (follow-up, 2026-08-18). The first is a bounding-box rejection when no template sample of any ring position can land inside the image. The second is a row-wise early exit that abandons a position once the rows still to come cannot lift its score to `SubFinderMinScore`. The reflectance-retry inversion pass also uses the shared `LuminanceInverter`. Since 2026-09-24, the positions from the fourth ring out are screened first on the half-module lattice they sample. Each lattice point is read once and serves every position. The template needs 24 of 25, so two certain mismatches drop a position, and all positions of a row drop at once in 64-bit masks. A point next to a pixel edge counts as a match either way, within a margin several times the float rounding between the screen's expression and the search's. So the answer is the unscreened search's, bit for bit. A point whose margin ends exactly on the image border is outside on both classification paths. Random frames never land on that float, so the comparison of the vector and scalar paths also places one point on each border (a strict comparison planted on one path had passed it). With the ring walk no longer visiting the interior of each ring, and with a branch-free, 128-bit classification of the lattice, a failing rMQR decode on a noise-like image is 4-7x faster. Against `main`, a detection miss on an adversarial image goes from 12.9 ms to 8.8 ms, and an ordinary non-QR image from 216 to 182 µs. The guards alone were worth more (14.2 ms → 4.7 ms, measured mid-branch), but the strideless retry that made detection correct costs a second scan pass per polarity | The 18-bit finder-side format copy passes random data about a quarter of the time, which is what lets the sub-finder search run dozens of times per image. Tightening it was measured and rejected (2026-09-23). Accepting only copies within 1 bit cut a failing decode on 1 px noise from 123 to 10 ms, but lost 457 sweep renders (170 within 2 bits). The lost renders are anti-aliased and bilinear ones below 2.5 px/module, and keystones past 6 %, whose copy reads 2-3 bits off at the unrefined frame. Using the edge timing rows as a second key was no better (up to 100 % wrong at the unrefined frame, for frames that went on to read). Budgeting sub-finder searches per candidate is untried |
| Finder candidate scan performance | A reference strideless sweep came first (it was sized for Micro QR), then the benchmark-driven follow-up (2026-08-17), corrected in review (2026-08-18). `FindCandidates` is a plain row-strided scan (stride 4) with no fallback of its own. When the strided pass reads nothing, the image decoders run the whole decode again through `FindCandidatesFullSweep`. The first design put the fallback inside the scan and triggered it on "no candidate confirmed on two or more rows". That is a statement about the image rather than about the symbol: a second QR code or a noise artefact satisfies it on the real symbol's behalf, and a differential sweep measured the loss. With the trigger moved to the caller, detection on an image of one symbol reads a strict superset of what a full sweep reads. After a read too long for the destination, the sweep does not run. That is a residual of the [single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan). The scan is shared with the Micro QR image decoder, and since 2026-10-01 it is one scan for both ([single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan)) | The strideless retry costs a second decode pipeline on every failing image. Since 2026-09-24 it skips a candidate equal to one that the strided pass already decoded without a settled result ([image decode passes](qrcode-symbologies.md#image-decode-passes)) |
| Luminance conversion performance | A reference per-pixel loop came first, then the benchmark-driven fast path (follow-up, 2026-08-17). That fast path is an AVX2 kernel at 32 px per iteration, bit-exact through the `pmaddubsw` weight split `[R,G,G,B] × [77,51,99,29]` (both pairs sum to 128, and the BT.601 weights sum to 256). It handles the row remainder in 8-px blocks plus one overlapping block, and it handles alpha in-vector. Then came the ARM64 tier (2026-08-19): a NEON kernel at 16 px per iteration built on UDOT. UDOT sums `77R + 150G + 29B` for four whole pixels without deinterleaving, and it weights the 4th byte 0, so RGB888x padding costs nothing. The NEON tier vectorizes *every* alpha shape, including arbitrary partial straight alpha, the case the AVX2 tier left scalar. It does so by classifying each row once and latching the mode, so four row modes ship rather than two. Then came a 128-bit tier (2026-09-30) for every other vector target: x64 without AVX2, WebAssembly, and ARM64 without the dot-product instructions. In it, R and B share 16-bit lanes and G has its own, weighted by a 16-bit multiply-add (SSE2 `pmaddwd`, WebAssembly's dot product, and a portable multiply and fold elsewhere). It uses the NEON tier's row modes. On WebAssembly, a partially transparent block uses the per-pixel formula, and a row in the composite mode uses the scalar loop, because the vector composite was slower there. Conversion alone against the scalar loop, on default NativeAOT, WebAssembly AOT and interpreted: opaque 0.21 to 0.22, 0.62 and 0.54 to 0.58; straight alpha 0.41, 1.00 and 1.01. A bitmap decode with the histogram's 128-bit tier: 0.33 to 0.42, 0.61 and 0.56 to 0.70. On ARM64 without the dot-product instructions (Apple M2: NativeAOT compiled without them, and the JIT under `DOTNET_EnableArm64Dp=0`; 2026-10-01), against the scalar path main ran there: opaque 0.44 to 0.51, straight alpha 0.71 to 0.76, and a bitmap decode 0.57 to 0.69. Where a core has the dot-product instructions, the dot-product tier stays about twice as fast. Shared by all three symbologies | The AVX2 tier still falls back to the scalar formula for the remainder of a partial-straight-alpha row, which the NEON tier vectorizes. That gap is worth closing with the exact identity `x / 255 == ((x + 1) * 257) >> 16`, at roughly 3x the operations of the opaque path. Also, a layout beyond BGRA / RGBA / RGB888x |
| Grid sampling performance | A reference scalar sampler came first, then three tiers (follow-up, 2026-08-20): `SampleGridSimd128` (projective), `SampleGridSimd128Affine`, and the scalar loop as both the parity reference and the fallback below Vector128. The affine tier is not a bet on typical input. `TryDecodeFrame` builds every frame before the perspective search with `perspectiveX = perspectiveY = 0`, so the denominator is exactly `1f`, and dropping both divisions changes no sampled byte. Measured: 2.4-3.8x on the kernel, -14 to -16 % on span image decode. Not shared with the Standard QR row kernel: that kernel multiplies by a single reciprocal where this one divides twice, so the two do not sample identical bytes | The gather sets the floor (0.70 ns/module, and NEON has no gather instruction), so the next step is a different data layout rather than a better kernel. Separately, axis-aligned sampling would gain a measured 6-10 % that is still available. That is cross-symbology work rather than an rMQR item |
| Too-small destination is terminal per finder candidate | The rule, the reason for it, and what it cost before are in the [single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan). That section also covers the skip of a candidate inside the symbol that read, and the re-read by coverage that rMQR alone still made, until 2026-10-01, after a read that did not fit | Accepted residual: 2 of 11,200 fuzzed noise frames report `DestinationTooSmall` with a one-character destination on an image holding no symbol. Revisit if a caller reports growing its buffer for an image with nothing in it |
| Codeword extraction performance | A reference per-module walk came first (Phase 6), then the benchmark-driven fast path (follow-up, 2026-08-17). Per-version tables are built once from the encoder's own predicates: the walk order with the mask fused in, plus a PEXT/PDEP descriptor per column pair. Four tiers use them. On x64 with AVX2 and fast BMI2, a bit-plane kernel transposes the grid into per-column bit planes, then runs one PEXT + PDEP per column. ARM64 has a pair-plane kernel (2026-08-20). x64 without fast PEXT, and WebAssembly, run the same pair planes on portable vectors (2026-10-01). Everywhere else, a portable table walk runs. ARM64 has no PEXT/PDEP, so the deposit step is designed out rather than emulated. One 32-bit lane holds a whole column *pair*, which is already that pair's output field with the function modules still in it, and a per-version run table compresses those modules out. The reference stays the source of truth for the tables, and all four tiers are checked against the naive reference | Extraction stops being a material share of matrix decode, or a symbol shape appears whose data mask is not a small number of runs per pair |

## Lessons learned

- With the encoder proven module-exact against two external lineages, the decoder round trip is a weak test on its own. The strong tests were the corpus (148 external symbols from both lineages, checking payload, version and ECC) and the damage classes: t errors per block corrected in every block of every version × ECC; t + 1 in one block never decoding cleanly; format copies damaged singly or jointly; a contradiction between format and dimensions; remainder bits ignored.
- The two format copies make the format decoder robust with no extra effort: one copy can be destroyed outright. The arbitration rule that holds up is "among the copies naming the version the dimensions give, the closer wins". The review found that arbitrating on distance alone first let a copy miscorrected toward another version's word (5+ errors landing within 3 of it) veto the valid copy. So the matrix decoder now feeds the version derived from the dimensions into the arbitration.
- Image detection on a wide symbol is a long-baseline problem. Everything measured at the finder is only good to a few percent, and a few percent of 139 modules is several modules. The design that worked makes the far anchor (the sub-finder) the authority for scale and rotation, and treats every locally measured quantity it overrides as an approximation. The perspective search's row pitch is the one quantity it does not override. That is why a scale a few percent off can still decide that search.
- The finder-side format read is the pipeline's first exit, and at low density it was the step that failed (2026-09-20). Below 2 px/module, a renderer that snaps modules to whole pixels gave the finder a scale 3.5-6 % over the symbol's. That is most of a pixel at the copy's column 11, so the version never read, and the sub-finder refinement that would have corrected the scale never ran.

  The read now tries the scales nearest the measured one (±2 to ±8 %) in turn, and it goes on while the frames built on them fail. It goes on because which finder modules the snapping widens depends on the orientation. A copy can therefore read exactly at a scale a few percent off (R11x77 at 137 px turned 270° reads its copy exactly at the measured scale) while the frame built on it still fails.

  Three rules bound that search. Each was measured rather than derived, and each trades reads against the time a failure takes:

  - A corrected scale must read an exact codeword. Accepting the usual 3-bit distance made a quarter of random reads a version, and the searches behind them made the no-symbol path 2.8× slower. Exact-only, it costs +2.5 %.
  - Scales are read only while the larger of the finder's two axes measures under 6 px per module. This is a cost bound, not an accuracy one. Lifting it would read more (renders whose sub-finder is hidden or carries as few as two wrong modules, and mildly keystoned ones), but it would make every other symbology's image fail more slowly: 2 to 2.8× on a Micro QR image and up to 2.5× on a Standard QR one.
  - The search stops once frames anchored on the sub-finder have read format information and failed. On a damaged symbol every scale reads the copy, and repeating those frames made the failure 3-5.3× slower.

  The unrefined frame is the exception and runs at every scale. Each scale is a different grid, and on a symbol whose sub-finder is hidden, the unrefined frame is the one that reads. Nothing cheaper separates a damaged symbol from a slightly wrong scale, since both fail in the data. The perspective search also takes its row pitch from the starting scale, so a later scale can rescue a mildly warped low-density render. Those renders are what the stop gives up.
- Test payloads must fit each version's capacity (R7x43-M holds 7 alphanumerics). The 13 early "decoder failures" were the generator rejecting the payload, and the decoder had passed everything.
- Extraction, ARM64 pair-plane tier (2026-08-20). Measured against the portable table walk on Apple M2: 0.30x at R17x139, 0.36x at R13x99, 0.55x at R11x59 and R7x139, and 0.92-0.94x at R7x43 and R11x27. There is no size switch, and the reason is a cost model rather than a boundary. The tier's cost per bit falls smoothly from 0.45 to 0.14 ns over a fixed floor of ~35 ns, while the portable walk costs ~0.48 ns/bit with no fixed cost. The two cross at about 100 bits, which is why the two smallest symbols win only 6-8 %. R7x139 was added to separate "small" from "short". A symbol with 5 data rows still wins 0.55x when it is wide, so the weak cases depend on total bits rather than height, and no height guard is needed.

  Rejected: unrolling every pair to its version's worst-case run count. A pair averages 1.0-2.3 runs, but the worst has 5-11, and unrolling measured 2.4x *slower* than the portable walk on small symbols. One flat run stream for the whole symbol removed that loss entirely. Deleting the 320-byte plane `stackalloc` was worth ~5 ns of zeroing alone, about 10 % of a small symbol. At 40-600 ns per call, the prologue is part of the hot loop.
- Extraction, 128-bit pair planes (2026-10-01). This is the ARM64 kernel on portable vectors, for x64 without fast PEXT and for WebAssembly, with NEON's three instructions replaced. A pair's two columns are adjacent bytes, so one 16-bit lane holds both, and `x | x >> 7` merges them where NEON unzips. The row insert is a shift and an OR where NEON has SLI. The row-reversed word takes four swap steps where NEON has RBIT and REV32, once a block. Against the table walk on a default NativeAOT publish, every version wins, from 0.21 at R17x139 to 0.71 at R7x43.

  On WebAssembly the sparse symbols lose (R7x43: 1.45 AOT-compiled and 1.47 interpreted). There the weak cases depend on stream bits per 8-column block, not on total bits. R7x139, 544 bits at 30 a block, loses interpreted at 1.05, while R13x43, 328 bits at 55 a block, wins at 0.92. WebAssembly uses the tier from 44 bits a block, the interpreter's break-even point (AOT-compiled code's lies between 27 and 33, and one flag gates both builds). R17x139 matrix decode takes 0.24 of its earlier time on default NativeAOT, 0.28 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.49 interpreted, the 128-bit syndrome pass included. The tier's flag is false on ARM64, whose own pair planes run first, so the dispatch there drops the branch.
- `TryCorrect` recomputes the syndromes after applying corrections, to catch silent miscorrection, so a corrected block runs the syndrome pass **twice**. That second pass is most of the gap between clean and corrected decodes (about 10 us of 12.8 us at R17x139). It is also why a faster syndrome kernel gains more on damaged input than on clean input: 6.47x against 4.10x when the ARM tier landed. Any estimate of correction cost from a clean-only benchmark will be wrong by roughly a factor of two.
- Correctable damage roughly doubles matrix decode time (279.6 → 554.9 ns at R7x43, 14.33 → 27.16 us at R17x139), so Berlekamp-Massey, Chien and Forney are about half of a damaged decode. The clean-only scenario set could not rank the correction path at all, which is why `RmQR_*_Corrected_Decode` exists. Its damage is accepted only when the decoder reports exactly the intended number of corrected errors, because flips that land on function patterns carry no codeword.
- One shipped correctness fix has **no discriminating test**. The perspective quadratic's `|sv|²` correction is verified analytically and numerically, but reverting it to `|v|²` keeps the keystone suite green, because the bias stays below the gates' tolerance. A synthetic sheared-frame probe of `TryPerspectiveVariants` would be that test.
- The qrtool tail defect in the corpus became a free robustness fixture. Those symbols decode with exactly one corrected codeword, so the fixture test asserts `ErrorsCorrected ≤ 1` for that lineage and `0` for libzint.
- Codeword extraction was the whole matrix decoder, not a part of it. The per-module `IsFunctionModule` predicate alone was 40-70 % of the extraction, and extraction was 70-91 % of `DecodeMatrix`, with Reed-Solomon correction under 1 %. Moving everything the walk derives from the version into cached tables was worth more than every instruction-level trick that followed (follow-up, 2026-08-17: 16-64x on the kernel, 5.0-8.0x on the matrix-decode API, -14 % on the image path, where detection dominates).
- The failure path has its own hot spots and must be profiled separately. None of the functions that three earlier optimization rounds targeted appears near the top of a failed decode. The cost was `TryLocateSubFinder`, which barely runs on the success path. It was called once for every frame the 18-bit format copy let through, and that gate passes random data about a quarter of the time (follow-up, 2026-08-18).
- Where an early exit is tested decides whether the fast path pays for it. The same algorithmic idea (abandon a template position once it cannot reach the acceptance floor) cost **+12 %** on the largest successful decode when tested per sample. The counter, the merged bounds condition and a `goto` out of two nested loops made the 25-sample loop slower for the positions that run it in full. Tested once per row of five, it cost nothing, and it still gave up after one row on the failing path. The kernel benchmark could not see this. Only the end-to-end run could.
- A fallback cannot make a stride safe unless its trigger asks a question about the symbol being looked for. While the fallback fired only on "found nothing", the finder scan's row stride could not be widened past the value `TryFind` uses, because a single false candidate would suppress the fallback. Changing the trigger to "nothing confirmed on two or more rows" was taken as licence for stride 6, because it appeared to make a too-coarse stride report itself. It does not. `Count >= 2` is evaluated over the whole candidate list, so it is a statement about the *image*, not about the symbol. A second QR code, a printed logo or salt-and-pepper noise confirms on its own, and suppresses exactly the pass the real symbol needed. A differential sweep against the pre-stride build measured the cost. Over 6,000 images carrying a second finder-like pattern, 69 decodes were lost against 26 gained, concentrated at 3-4 px/module under rotation. Over the same images without one, there were 0 divergences. `TryFind` is not exposed to this, because its trigger ("no consistent triple") is a question about the symbol.
- The first repair attempt was to make the stride itself safe, and measurement rejected it. Requiring the stride to land in every band means measuring the band. The band turns out to be 3 modules tall only while the symbol is axis-aligned. Under rotation the run ratios drift off-centre, and the surviving band narrows to a floor of 5 rows at 3 px/module, which means stride 4 rather than 6. But the same sweep showed that tightening the stride while replacing the trigger with "the candidate list is empty" was worse overall than the code it replaced (net −29 / −77 / −25 across the three corpora, against −8 / −43 / −3). The reason is that an empty list almost never happens: any stray dark run anywhere produces a candidate, so that fallback is close to dead code. Testing the two changes one at a time is what showed this. The stride change alone was an improvement, and the trigger change alone was the worst variant measured.
- What made it sound was moving the widening out of the scan entirely. No signal available inside a flat candidate list is about the symbol. The one question that is, "did anything actually decode", belongs to the image decoders. They now run the strided scan, and run the whole decode again through a strideless sweep when nothing decoded. By construction, that restores exact parity with a full sweep on an image of one symbol (0 regressions over 15,980 images). It keeps the strided scan on every successful decode, and pays for the sweep only on images that were going to fail. It is the same shape `TryFind` always had, where the trigger is "no consistent triple". The lesson is that a fallback is only as sound as the question that triggers it, and a scan that returns candidates cannot ask a question about a symbol.
- The image path's largest single cost was never rMQR-specific. Grayscale conversion was 69 % of `TryDecode(SKBitmap)` on both the smallest and the largest symbol. No benchmark went through that entry point, so the cost was invisible until one was added (follow-up, 2026-08-17: 14-30× on the conversion, `TryDecode(SKBitmap)` -68 to -69 %, converter share now 7-15 %). Measure the entry points users call, not only the ones that are convenient to feed.
- Exactness can come from the coefficients rather than from wider arithmetic. The BT.601 weights sum to 256, and that one fact does three things. It lets a `pmaddubsw` pair split stay under saturation (51 + 99 for green makes both pairs exactly 128). It keeps the whole weighted sum inside 16 bits unsigned. And it makes the premultiplied composite collapse to a single add on the luminance. A formula's constants are part of what makes it vectorizable.
- A fast path that handles only the regular case leaves its own guard as the bottleneck. Splitting column pairs into "clean" (both columns data on every row) and "irregular" covered only 39-45 % of the bits on the 27-wide versions. The transpose was paid in full while most bits still went through a per-bit loop, and those versions regressed against the plain table walk. PEXT and PDEP take arbitrary masks, so an irregular pair is the same two instructions with different constants. Deleting the split removed the regression and was the largest single win after the tables.
- A test that derives its expectation from the API under test stops being a test of it. `Damage_WithinCorrectionCapacity` originally flipped `ECCPerBlock / 2` codewords per block (the Reed-Solomon strength), so it was the only thing that checked "rMQR reserves no `p`". Rewriting it to call `GetErrorCorrectionCapacity` made it agree with any capacity, however wrong. Injecting `capacity - 1` left all 133 robustness tests green while the decoder silently refused corrections the code could make, and only the test of the constants' values caught it. Damage tests must be written against the property being claimed (what RS can do), not against the constant that claims it.
- An unread specification table stays unread no matter how the code is restructured. Moving the capacity rule into a named function and a 64-row table made the decoder better factored but added no knowledge. The doc changes that came with it turned an honest open question into an asserted fact whose stated source (Table 8) had never been read. What actually closed the gap was measuring the reference implementation (`probe-rmqr-capacity`, both directions, 64/64). Restructuring is not evidence. Record the provenance you actually have, and keep the revisit trigger pointed at the evidence you still lack.
- The anisotropic grid is kept for crisp renders whose rows are under 2 px, not for anything inside the measured envelope. Non-square modules are handled before it: the frame measures each axis on its own, and the isotropic grid scales that frame uniformly. So on non-square renders up to 1.65:1 either way (short side 3 to 8 px, every version, right angles), the anisotropic grid never ran.

  It was switched off over the envelope (2026-09-27: the test suite and about 49,000 renders of every version, clean, rotated, mirrored, non-square and keystoned, crisp and anti-aliased). It had been the first grid to read on 61 inputs, and without it another grid read 60 of them. The one lost is R15x43 at 1.5 px, anti-aliased, mirrored and turned 45°, where neighbouring angles already fail. As the gate to the perspective search, it never decided a read.

  It does decide crisp renders with rows of 1.6 to 1.95 px and columns of 2.5 to 4 px (1.43:1 to 2.3:1): 105 of 8,684 reads. The reason is not the modules' shape. On R11x77 at 3.05 × 1.95 px, the finder measures rows of 2.0 px, and the sub-finder lands 0.25 px above its snapped centre row. So the isotropic grid turns 0.38° and misses the far rows. The anisotropic grid has no turn, and its row scale, though 10 % short, still puts all eleven rows on their pixels. Neither alternative replaces it there. Centring the sub-finder on its ring edges reads that input but still loses 76 of the 8,684 reads. The unrefined frame, which keeps the finder's column scale (1.6 % short), reads 2.

  It costs one grid wherever the isotropic grid fails with a sub-finder found: 16 to 24 % of a keystone read with the left edge shortened, and 1.5 to 3.5 % with the top shortened. Failing decodes do not change.
- An edge is located at the midpoint of the two levels, never at the threshold (2026-09-28). On an image of only 0 and 255, the Otsu threshold is 1, one level above the dark one. A crossing there puts every edge on the centre of its dark pixel, half a pixel into the dark. On crisp keystoned renders at 8 px/module, the finder's outline came out 6 to 7 % large, and its format copies did not read. The histogram pass that finds the threshold already has both levels, so the edge level costs nothing. Computed in a pass of its own, it cost a small clean read 4 %.
- Chords across a finder must stay off the edge of its centre square. Seeded 0.75 module apart, the outer chords ran along that edge, whose grey pixels cross the level. Chords half a module apart from the seed, then a module apart along the outline's own axes, cross the ring squarely and halve the axis error (median 0.62° → 0.32°). And a finder measured at under 2.5 px/module through chords two modules long shows up to 8° of shear when it has none, so the 3° gate judges the second measurement.
- A search that stops at the first hit should start sampling where the answer probably is. The trace predicts each edge within a sample or two. A crossing search that scanned its whole window cost 69 ns. Sampling outward from the middle, and stopping once no pair further out can be nearer, costs 42 and finds the same crossing to the bit. A trace of R17x139 at 8 px/module went from 44 to 20 µs.
- A variant measured on a set that every variant reads says nothing. The strong keystones read 575 of 576 whichever guard was switched off, so each guard looked dead. The same keystones at 2-3 px/module, blurred and with noise, told the parts apart. They led to moving both end windows to a module (0.5 and 0.4 before) and to removing the step's anchor on the last run, which then cost reads. Each change shifted what the others decide, so every part was measured again on the final code, and the renders each part's test checks were chosen again.
- Timing needs the JIT held fixed. With tiered compilation on, the builds before and after this change measured 109 and 410 µs over the same images, a difference that neither build's code caused. With tiered compilation off and the two runs interleaved, both measured about 100.
- Work a search skips, and a result that ends a search, both need measuring. Skipping a trace because another frame of the finder had already traced that side cost 35 of 800 noisy keystones. The start decides a trace, and the second start was the one that read. And a traced grid that got past its format information and failed, when counted as the frame's result, ended the search over scales at 1.3 px/module, before the scale whose anchored grid reads.
- **A search over positions that share their samples is a search over the samples** (2026-09-24). A failing decode on 512 × 512 noise spent 87 % of its time in `TryLocateSubFinder`. The 2,601 positions of one lean on the widest symbol read the same 3,481 half-module lattice points, up to 25 times each. Now each point is classified once, as dark, light, outside or edge. A position with two certain mismatches cannot reach the 24 of 25 it needs, and whole rows of positions drop at once in 64-bit masks. The first three rings are scored as before, since a sub-finder near its prediction is found before the screen pays for itself. Exactness came from a margin, not from reproducing the float expression: a point within a few roundings of a pixel edge counts as a match either way.

  Removing the dominant cost exposed two costs that no profile of the old code showed. The ring walk visited the interior of every ring (O(r³)), and on texture the pixel branch mispredicted half the time (1.5x on its own). Per lever on 8-bit noise: the screen 2.0x, with the ring walk 2.6x, the vector classification 3.5x, the branch-free read 5.4x, and with the sweep skip 6.3x end to end. The search itself went from 221 to 17 ms a decode (13x). Every result is unchanged.
- **The true-transform column ([qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#image-decode-sweep)) says the frame, not which frame.** Every keystoned render that failed did read through the geometry it was drawn with. That ruled out the pixels before anything was built, but the column could not say which frame would read them. The answer was where the symbol keeps its own geometry: its timing-pattern perimeter.
- **Two format copies hide a fault in reading one** (2026-09-29). When the matrix decoder's reader walked a copy's block by rows, or read the finder side's last three bits on the sub-finder side, every round trip still read, from the other copy. Only `RmQRCodeDecoderRobustnessTest`, which damages one copy, failed. So a test of a format reader damages the copy it does not read, or reads each bit alone, as `RmQRFormatPositionTest` does for both readers. The matrix decoder's test came on 2026-09-30. Before it, a reader that never read the finder-side copy's last bit had passed every other test. That bit is the level bit, which reads 1 in every H symbol. Under that reader, an H symbol whose sub-finder copy is destroyed still reads, but stops reading once its finder-side copy carries three bit errors, which the correct reader corrects.
- **A position helper asked per bit cost a percent where the reader runs** (2026-09-29). The format positions are stated once, in `RmQRConstants`. Asking for each bit's module measured about 1 % slower in two places: on an image that does not read, where the image decoder's reader runs for every frame tried, and on a clean R17x139 matrix. Marking the helper for aggressive inlining did not recover the loss. Both readers walk the block from `GetFormatBlock` with their own loops. Only the placer asks per bit, and it writes a cached template once per version and level. On default NativeAOT, the matrix decoder's reader still called `GetFormatBlock` and `GetFormatTail`, which the JIT inlines but ILC did not. Both are marked `AggressiveInlining` since 2026-10-01. That took `ReadFormatCopies` from 127 to 105 instructions on x64, and from 125 to 103 on ARM64.
